passage: I had my speech ready to tell Amma and Papa about the design course in Bengaluru. Before saying it, I tried it out on my friend Pankaj over chai. "What do your parents fear?" Pankaj asked. I laughed. "Nothing. They'll just be sad." "Are you sure?" I thought about it all the way home. Amma always said cities are lonely. Papa worried about who would look after me if I fell ill. I had never thought about either. I added a new line: "I'll come home every second month, and you can call me any evening." When I told them on Sunday, Amma's shoulders came down, and Papa asked about the hostel. It was not easy, but it was a conversation, not a quarrel. - Usha

qa.a: Amma may have felt relieved and reassured, as the shoulders coming down suggests.

subtype: Approach: asking a trusted friend or counsellor to help prepare [Action]
passage:
Counselling note, campus wellbeing centre, 4 February.
Lakshmi came in to prepare for telling her parents she is taking a job in Singapore. Her message was clear: the offer, the salary, the growth, the joining date. It was well organised.
I asked one question: "What do you think your parents are most afraid of?" She paused a long time. Then she said, "That I won't come back. That they'll be old and alone in Madurai." She had not considered that at all; she had been preparing to defend the job.
We worked on one extra line together: "I'll come home every Pongal and for two weeks each summer, and we'll video call on Sundays." She wrote it at the top of her notes, above the salary. She left saying she felt less as if she were walking into an exam. Follow-up in two weeks.
— Ujjwal

qa.a: "I'll come home every Pongal and for two weeks each summer, and we'll video call on Sundays."

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when she paused a long time?
qa.a: She was surprised and a little shaken to realise she hadn't considered her parents' fear of being left alone.

qa.q: Why is putting the reassurance above the salary a good choice?
qa.a: It answers her parents' real fear first, so they can take in the rest of the news without feeling abandoned.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's parents hear the message now?
qa.a: They may still be sad, but the promise of visits and Sunday calls would ease their fear of being old and alone in Madurai.

grounding: It shows a young woman preparing with a counsellor who asks what her parents fear, leading her to add a reassurance about visits to her message.

passage:
Pema's diary, Wednesday.
Practised the big talk with Aditi at the momo place after work. I did my whole speech about the Mumbai job: the studio, the pay, how it's a real career. Aditi listened, then said, "Okay, but what are Ama and Pala actually scared of?"
I started to say "that I'll fail" and stopped. It isn't that. It's that I'm the only one left in Gangtok since my brother went to Bengaluru. They're scared of an empty house. Of festivals with just the two of them.
So I've added something to the start of the talk: "I'll be home every Losar, and I'll take leave in October to help at Aunty's farm." It's true. I'd just never said it.
Strangely, I'm less nervous now. It feels less like a fight and more like a plan.

qa.a: "What are Ama and Pala actually scared of?"

qa.q: Why is Pema less nervous now?
qa.a: Pema feels relieved because the talk now answers Ama and Pala's real fear, so it feels less like a fight and more like a plan.

qa.q: What else could Pema do after the talk?
qa.a: Pema could agree a regular call time with Ama and Pala and book the October leave early so the promise is kept.

qa.q: What are Ama and Pala likely to feel when they hear the new opening?
qa.a: They may still feel sad, but reassured that festivals like Losar won't be spent alone.
